problems.description: Static analysis flags module-level constants that should be UPPER_CASE in registry.py, server.py, and broker.py
Static analysis flags classes that should use PascalCase in app.py, test_integration.py, test_notification_server.py, and test_rate_limit_history.py
SonarQube reports 3 code smells and +26 cognitive complexity, concentrated in the message-routing path (_on_message / broadcast / direct dispatch)

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: connection state isolated in ClientRegistry vs orchestration/messaging in NotificationServer
Comprehensive docstrings including a module-level wire-format spec for the message types
Thread-safe registry with a lock guarding every operation
Correct lifecycle handling: start/stop plus finally-based cleanup on disconnect
Type hints on public signatures (snake_case functions, PascalCase classes as required)
commit_reviews.summary: Strong greenfield foundation — well-documented, cleanly separated server and registry modules — with only minor case-convention flags (measured convention 0.80) and a small cognitive-complexity bump in the routing path.

problems.description: unsubscribe() discards from the channel member set but never removes empty entries from _client_channels, leaving stale empty sets behind — inconsistent with remove(), which fully cleans up both maps. This desync risk grows the dual-map (client→channels / channel→clients) cleanup logic.

Measured cognitive complexity +35 and +6 smells on a +362-line change: _on_message is a growing if/elif dispatch chain with channel-extraction and broadcast-overload branching. A dispatch table keyed by message type would contain the complexity as more channel/control message types accrue.

connections_for_channel returns an untyped bare 'list' while every sibling snapshot method in the module uses typed generics (List[str], Dict[str, int], Set[str]) — a small deviation from the file's own typing convention.

Measured convention score 0.80 with 9 violations (Classes should use PascalCase; Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE across app.py, broker.py, registry.py, server.py, and three test files). The diff introduces no module-level constants or classes, so these are pre-existing repo-state violations, not introduced by this commit.

strengths: Backward-compatible broadcast(payload, channel=None) keeps the existing API contract intact while extending it with optional channel targeting.
remove() correctly tears down both the client and its channel memberships under the single lock, keeping the two index maps consistent on disconnect.
Thread-safety is preserved by routing all new registry operations through the existing threading.Lock — matching the established pattern.
subscribers() returns a sorted snapshot, giving deterministic behavior, and all snapshot accessors return copies to avoid exposing mutable internals.
Clear docstrings on every new method and message type, and consistent snake_case/typed-signature style with the surrounding code.
commit_reviews.summary: The channel-subscription feature is well-integrated into the existing lock-guarded registry/server architecture with backward-compatible APIs, but introduces minor technical debt via dual-map cleanup inconsistency and a measured spike in message-handler complexity (+35 cognitive complexity, +6 smells).

problems.description: Cognitive complexity increased by +61 with 2 new code smells in a single commit (mostly the broker listener loop, dynamic query_history WHERE building, and cleanup_expired branching); the logic is correct but hard to follow.
MessageStore.cleanup_expired loads every row from the messages table, parses each timestamp in Python, then issues one DELETE per expired row — O(n) scan plus per-row writes on the full history.
MessageStore opens a fresh sqlite3 connection and ConnectionState/RateLimiter a fresh Redis connection on every call instead of reusing pooled connections, which adds overhead on hot paths.
Broad exception swallowing (`except Exception: continue` in _listen, `except Exception: pass` in start/stop) silently drops handler errors and connection failures, making failures hard to diagnose.
broker.py bundles four distinct concerns into one module (pub/sub backbone, SQLite persistence, connection-state mirroring, rate limiting); the classes are clean but the module cohesion is broad.
publish() does not catch redis.RedisError while ping() does, so a downed broker raises into the caller rather than surfacing a graceful status.

9 lint violations (measured score 0.80): module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in broker.py, registry.py, server.py and test_notification_server.py; non-PascalCase classes in app.py and the test files. All are naming nits, not structural problems.

strengths: Coherent distributed design: Redis pub/sub fan-out across instances, SQLite durable history, Redis-mirrored connection state for restart re-hydration, and distributed per-client rate limiting.

Clean separation of concerns across MessageStore, ConnectionState, RateLimiter, and MessageBroker, integrated through a clean import seam in server.py that respects the existing pluggable architecture.
Env-driven configuration (REDIS_URL, DATABASE_URL, RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) with sensible defaults consistent with the codebase style.
Substantial integration coverage (test_integration.py, +352 lines) exercising the new backbone, plus parameterized SQL with no injection risk.
0 bugs and 0 duplications per SonarQube, with robust JSON payload decoding and timestamp normalization helpers.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3's integration lands a sound, well-tested Redis/SQLite backbone that respects the codebase's patterns, but introduces notable maintainability debt (cognitive complexity +61, connection-per-call I/O, O(n) cleanup) and 9 minor naming-convention violations (score 0.80).

problems.description: Incomplete decoupling: despite the transport-agnostic claim, NotificationServer.process_request still imports and depends on websockets HTTP types (Headers, Request, Response) to serve the REST endpoints, so a swapped-in non-WebSocket transport would still need websockets HTTP handling.

Cognitive complexity rose +5: the env-var transport selection (create_transport factory) plus the transport.start/stop/broadcast/send dispatch adds branching that offsets some of the simplification from the -73 line reduction.

The pluggable transport abstraction (TRANSPORT env var, BaseTransport, factory) is speculative generality: only WebSocket exists today, and no concrete SSE/polling/TCP transport is added, so the seam is currently unexercised.
server.py still triggers the 'module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' SonarQube violation; it predates this commit, but the refactor touched this file and did not correct it.

strengths: Clean dependency-inversion: the core notification logic (broker/registry/store coordination, broadcast/direct routing, membership restore) is now transport-agnostic and delegates all client I/O to BaseTransport.

Good DI seam: the transport parameter plus the create_transport factory keyed on TRANSPORT makes selection explicit and overridable for tests, while keep-alive/message-format helpers (utc_now_iso, make_message, dumps_message) were consolidated into the transport module instead of being duplicated.
Net reduction of ~73 lines in server.py with the wire-format and connection-loop responsibilities moved out, and the existing broker/registry/store separation is preserved unchanged.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, convention-following refactor that cleanly abstracts the transport layer behind BaseTransport with a factory + DI seam, improving modularity and reducing technical debt, though the retained websockets HTTP handling means the decoupling is only partial and the +5 cognitive complexity is worth watching.

problems.description: cleanup_expired loads every row into memory and deletes row-by-row in Python; a single 'DELETE FROM messages WHERE timestamp < cutoff' would be O(1) memory and one round trip. Fine for small tables but scales poorly.

Inconsistent time handling: query_history filters via lexicographic SQL string comparison ('timestamp >= ?') while cleanup_expired parses to tz-aware datetimes; the string form is only correct if all stored timestamps are uniformly normalized UTC isoformat.
SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +35 for the change; the branching in query_history/cleanup_expired could be flattened to reduce the smell.
RateLimiter uses the synchronous redis.Redis while server.py is asyncio-based, so check() blocks the event loop; this matches the existing ConnectionState pattern but may contend under load.

strengths: Extracting _decode removes duplicated JSON-parsing logic across list_messages and query_history
RateLimiter follows the existing Redis-backed service-class pattern and enforces limits consistently across instances sharing a broker channel
Robust _parse_iso helper correctly handles Z suffixes and naive timestamps, defaulting to UTC
query_history returning (messages, has_more) enables clean pagination without an extra count query
Env-var config with sane defaults (MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS, RATE_LIMIT) matches the existing configuration convention
commit_reviews.summary: A feature-complete commit that cleanly extends the existing Redis/SQLite architecture with cross-instance rate limiting and history/retention, respects established patterns, and refactors duplication; the measured 0.80 convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations in app.py/registry.py/tests rather than the new code, whose own classes and helpers are properly named.

compounding_issues: Stale seed app.py (unrelated Flask Todo API) was never removed — the agent built a parallel notification stack and left the orphaned seed file in the tree across all 5 sessions
The _on_message if/elif dispatch chain grew unbounded: cognitive complexity compounded each session (+26, +35, +61, +5, +35), and the S2 suggestion to use a dispatch table was never adopted

Connection-per-call anti-pattern: MessageStore opens a fresh sqlite3 connection and ConnectionState/RateLimiter fresh Redis connections on every call — flagged in S3, never pooled, still present in S5
Repo hygiene: __pycache__ bytecode (S1) and messages.db (S4) were committed to git and never cleaned

Pre-existing convention violations (module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, non-PascalCase classes in app.py/tests) were re-flagged every session yet never corrected, pinning measured convention score at ~0.80
cleanup_expired loads all rows and deletes one-by-one while query_history filters via lexicographic timestamp string comparison — the O(n) retention path flagged in S3 persisted into S5
key_decisions: Choosing websockets + asyncio (not Flask-SocketIO) with a thread-safe ClientRegistry as the single source of truth for connection state
Establishing a canonical JSON wire format {type, payload, timestamp} with type-based dispatch in S1, extended backward-compatibly (optional channel param) rather than breaking the API contract

Adopting Redis pub/sub as the shared message backbone with Redis-mirrored connection state and SQLite message history in S3 — the distributed substrate that S5's cross-instance rate limiting builds on
Extracting a pluggable BaseTransport + create_transport factory with a DI seam in S4, making the core transport-agnostic and reducing server.py by ~73 lines
Implementing distributed per-client rate limiting via Redis counters in S5, following the established Redis-backed service-class pattern
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 laid a strong, well-documented foundation (clean registry/server separation, thread-safe connection handling, 14 passing tests) despite the degraded seed spec and a mismatched Todo-API seed. Session 2 added channels and REST endpoints but introduced a growing dispatch chain and a stale-set bug flagged as the first real technical debt. Session 3 made the biggest architectural jump — Redis pub/sub fan-out, SQLite history, and connection-state rehydration — at the cost of the session's worst complexity spike (+61) and connection-per-call overhead. Session 4 was the quality inflection: a genuine refactor that inverted the transport dependency behind BaseTransport, removed ~73 lines from server.py, reached the highest architectural-fit score (0.90), and introduced no new debt. Session 5 completed the system with cross-instance rate limiting, history/retention endpoints, and a small dedup refactor, respecting all established patterns. Test coverage grew monotonically (14→25→40→40→57, all green at the end) and code expanded from 366 to 1,279 lines, with measured convention score flat at ~0.80 due to persistent pre-existing violations rather than new code.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session build that progressed from greenfield server to channel routing to a Redis/SQLite distributed backbone to a clean transport abstraction and finally cross-cutting rate limiting and persistence, with quality trending upward and only minor, pre-existing hygiene and complexity issues left unresolved.
